meta.titre: Opportunity Cost: the price of every choice and the production possibility curve
meta.sous_theme: Opportunity cost, production possibility curve, efficiency and increasing opportunity cost

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader in Bafoussam who closes her stall for a day to attend a training course loses more than the course fee. She also gives up the sales she would have made that day. Every choice, whether by a household, a firm or a government, means giving up something else, and economists call the value of what is given up the opportunity cost. The production possibility curve turns this idea into a picture of what a whole economy can produce. Examiners use it to test whether you can read points on and off the curve, explain its shape and judge efficiency.

items: Resources are scarce relative to wants, so choices must be made.
Factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Output of a good can be measured in physical units such as tonnes.

sections.titre: Opportunity cost and the production possibility curve
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Opportunity cost
**Opportunity cost** is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made. It is measured in the forgone benefit, which may be money, goods or time, and it differs from the money cost because it includes benefits that are given up even when no payment is made. Only what is actually given up because of the choice counts: a meal the trader would have bought anyway is not part of the cost of attending a course.

### The production possibility curve
A **production possibility curve (PPC)** shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce in a given period when all resources are fully and efficiently used and technology is fixed. It can be described by a table of values.

| Position of a point | Meaning |
|---|---|
| On the curve | Resources fully employed and used efficiently (productive efficiency); output cannot rise in one good without falling in the other |
| Inside the curve | Resources unemployed or used inefficiently; output of one or both goods can rise |
| Outside the curve | Unattainable with present resources and technology |

Moving along the curve, the opportunity cost of one good is the amount of the other that must be sacrificed. The **marginal opportunity cost** of a good is the quantity of the other good lost per extra unit gained.

### Shape of the curve
Most PPCs are **concave to the origin** (bowed outward), reflecting **increasing opportunity cost**: resources are not equally suited to both goods, so as more of one good is produced, resources that are less and less suitable must be switched to it and ever more of the other good is lost per unit gained. If resources were equally adaptable, the PPC would be a straight line with a constant opportunity cost.

### Shifts of the curve
**Economic growth** shifts the curve outward, through more resources, better quality of resources or improved technology. Technology that improves the production of only one good moves the curve outward along that good's axis only. A fall in the resources of the economy, for example through a natural disaster, shifts it inward. Moving from a point inside the curve towards the curve is different: it is the better use of existing resources (sometimes called actual growth), and the curve itself does not move.

variantes.nom: Table-reading question (cost per step and efficiency)
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a table of combinations of two goods is given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Subtract neighbouring values of the sacrificed good, divide by the gain in the other good, and show that the cost rises (or is constant). To locate a point, compare it with the value on the curve for the same quantity of one good.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a decision by a firm, household or government is described.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Add the cash cost and the value of the best forgone use of time or resources, but leave out spending that would have happened anyway. State the opportunity cost in the same units.

variantes.nom: Evaluation question (how useful is the concept?)
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word is discuss or to what extent.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Explain that it forces all alternatives to be considered, then note that benefits forgone are hard to measure and that values differ between people, so decisions involve judgement.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Suppose an economy produces only cocoa and maize and has the following PPC, in thousand tonnes per year.

| Combination | Cocoa | Maize |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 80 |
| B | 10 | 72 |
| C | 20 | 60 |
| D | 30 | 40 |
| E | 40 | 0 |

(a) Calculate the opportunity cost, in maize, of each extra 10 thousand tonnes of cocoa, and say what this shows about the shape of the curve.
(b) Calculate the average opportunity cost of one tonne of cocoa when output moves from 10 to 30 thousand tonnes.
(c) Is the combination of 20 cocoa and 50 maize attainable? Is it efficient? What about 30 cocoa and 50 maize?
(d) Describe the effect of a new technique that increases only maize output.

etapes.action: Find the maize lost at each step.
etapes.justification: The opportunity cost of extra cocoa is the maize sacrificed.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A to B: $80-72=8$; B to C: $72-60=12$; C to D: $60-40=20$; D to E: $40-0=40$ thousand tonnes of maize.

etapes.justification: The cost of each extra 10 thousand tonnes of cocoa rises.
etapes.resultat_markdown: This is increasing opportunity cost, so the PPC is concave to the origin.

etapes.action: Average cost from 10 to 30 thousand tonnes of cocoa.
etapes.justification: Divide the maize sacrificed by the cocoa gained.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $\frac{72-40}{30-10}=\frac{32}{20}=1.6$ thousand tonnes of maize per thousand tonnes of cocoa.

etapes.action: Locate the two points relative to the curve.
etapes.justification: At 20 cocoa the curve shows 60 maize; at 30 cocoa it shows 40 maize.
etapes.resultat_markdown: (20, 50) has less maize than the curve, so it is inside: attainable, but not efficient. (30, 50) has more maize than the curve, so it is outside: unattainable.

etapes.action: Describe the shift caused by the new technique.
etapes.justification: A technique that raises only maize output does not change the maximum cocoa output.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The curve shifts outward on the maize axis only, so the maximum maize rises, the maximum cocoa stays at 40 thousand tonnes, and the curve pivots.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) The opportunity cost of each extra 10 thousand tonnes of cocoa is 8, 12, 20 and 40 thousand tonnes of maize, which rises, so the PPC is concave. (b) The average cost is 1.6 thousand tonnes of maize per thousand tonnes of cocoa. (c) The combination (20, 50) is attainable but inefficient because it lies inside the curve, and (30, 50) is unattainable with present resources. (d) The new technique pivots the curve outward along the maize axis while the maximum cocoa output stays at 40 thousand tonnes.

items.erreur_markdown: The opportunity cost of attending a course is only the fee paid.
items.pourquoi_faux: The money paid ignores the benefits given up, such as the income lost from not working that day.
items.correction_markdown: Add the cash cost and the value of the best forgone alternative.

items.erreur_markdown: Every point inside the PPC is unattainable.
items.pourquoi_faux: Points inside the curve are attainable but show unemployed or inefficiently used resources; points outside are unattainable.
items.correction_markdown: Write: on the curve means efficient, inside means inefficient, outside means unattainable.

items.erreur_markdown: Moving from a point inside the PPC to a point on it is an outward shift of the curve.
items.pourquoi_faux: That movement uses spare resources and does not raise the productive capacity of the economy; the curve itself has not moved.
items.correction_markdown: Describe an outward shift of the PPC as growth in productive capacity, caused by more or better resources or improved technology, and the move towards the curve as better use of existing resources.

items.erreur_markdown: The PPC is a straight line because opportunity cost is always the same.
items.pourquoi_faux: A straight line applies only when resources are equally suited to both goods; most economies show rising costs, giving a concave curve.
items.correction_markdown: Explain that unequal suitability of resources produces increasing opportunity cost and a bowed-out curve.

items.enonce_markdown: A trader in Bafoussam closes her stall for one day to attend a training course. She would have made a profit of 25,000 FCFA that day, the course fee is 10,000 FCFA and the transport costs 3,000 FCFA. She would have spent 2,000 FCFA on lunch at home either way. Calculate the opportunity cost of attending the course.
items.solution_markdown: The profit forgone, the fee and the transport all result from the choice: $25{,}000+10{,}000+3{,}000=$ **38,000 FCFA**. The lunch would have been bought anyway, so it is not counted.

items.enonce_markdown: An economy produces tea and beans (thousand tonnes). Its PPC passes through these combinations of (tea, beans): (0, 90), (10, 86), (20, 76), (30, 56) and (40, 0). (a) Calculate the opportunity cost, in beans, of each extra 10 thousand tonnes of tea. (b) Calculate the beans given up when tea rises from 0 to 20. (c) State whether (20, 80) and (20, 70) are attainable and which is efficient.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The beans lost are $90-86=4$, $86-76=10$, $76-56=20$ and $56-0=56$ thousand tonnes, so the cost **rises**.

(b) $90-76=$ **14 thousand tonnes of beans**.

(c) At 20 tea the curve shows 76 beans. (20, 80) has more beans than the curve and is **unattainable**. (20, 70) is inside the curve, so it is **attainable but not efficient**; the efficient point is (20, 76).

items.enonce_markdown: Discuss to what extent the concept of opportunity cost helps a government to choose between building a hospital and building a stadium. (8 marks)
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for the following points.

- Definition applied: building one means giving up the next best use of the same funds, so the real cost of the hospital is the benefit of the stadium forgone and vice versa (2 marks).
- Usefulness: it forces all alternatives to be compared, includes non-money benefits such as health or leisure, and discourages treating a project as free because it is funded by borrowing or donors (2 marks).
- Limits: the forgone benefits are hard to measure and compare, they differ across groups and over time, and a project's wider effects (jobs, health, tourism) are uncertain (2 marks).
- Complementary tools: cost-benefit analysis and public consultation turn the concept into numbers and value judgements (1 mark).
- Judgement: the concept shows what is at stake but cannot decide the choice alone (1 mark).

items_markdown: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone; costs that would be incurred anyway are not included.
A PPC shows the maximum combinations of two goods with fixed resources and technology: on the curve is efficient, inside is inefficient or unemployed, outside is unattainable.
A concave PPC reflects increasing opportunity cost because resources are not equally suited to both goods; a straight line means constant cost.
Economic growth shifts the PPC outward; better use of existing resources moves the economy towards the curve.
Opportunity cost is a powerful decision tool, but benefits forgone are hard to measure and involve value judgements.
